query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Multi-step forging of the eutectic lamellar-colony high-entropy alloy at moderate temperatures (≈600–700 °C), followed by a short sub-solvus anneal, will refine the lamellar spacing and stabilize colony boundaries, thereby suppressing microcrack initiation and enhancing dislocation slip transfer across colony interfaces. This will simultaneously increase yield strength and improve room-temperature tensile ductility compared to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies of B2/fcc phases prone to microcracking under tensile loading at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Perform multi-step forging at moderate temperatures (600–700 °C) under controlled strain, immediately followed by a short-duration sub-solvus anneal to partially recrystallize and stabilize the refined lamellar colonies.
generation.conditions: Forging steps conducted at ~600–700 °C with incremental strains, then annealing below the eutectic or B2 solvus temperature for a brief time (e.g., 30–60 min) to relieve residual stress and refine sub-grain boundaries. The as-processed material would be cooled to room temperature for final property assessment under uniaxial tensile loading.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced lamellar colony size and stabilized internal boundaries produced by controlled thermomechanical deformation and partial recrystallization.
generation.mechanism: Diminished defect sizes and improved phase boundary cohesion suppress microcrack initiation, and refined colony and lamellar dimensions facilitate progressive dislocation slip transfer across boundaries, increasing both yield strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Higher yield strength and tensile elongation at room temperature compared to the baseline unmodified lamellar structure, evidenced by reduced microcrack density and increased strain to failure.
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic lamellar-colony alloy with higher propensity for boundary microcracking and limited tensile ductility at room temperature.
generation.boundary: Requires forging temperatures near but below the material’s melting or eutectic temperature to avoid excessive grain growth; forging strain and subsequent annealing time must be controlled to stabilize the refined lamellar microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: Exact forging temperature–time–strain schedule may require optimization; excessive deformation or annealing may lead to coarsening or unexpected phase transformations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample sets of the same eutectic high-entropy alloy composition: one as-cast (unmodified baseline) and one subjected to multi-step moderate-temperature forging and short sub-solvus annealing under the specified conditions. Conduct uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature for both sets to compare mechanical behavior and microstructural evolution via postmortem microscopy.
measurements: Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and tensile elongation at fracture
Fractography and microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to evaluate crack nucleation and lamellar morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If forged-and-annealed samples do not exhibit higher ultimate tensile strength and increased tensile elongation (or if microcracking remains prevalent) relative to the unmodified baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), or multi-principal-element alloys, emerge as a new research frontier in the metallic materials community [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] . HEAs differentiate with conventional alloys in th

Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

chosen.why: A testable hypothesis is that multi-step thermomechanical reduction of lamellar colony size through forging at moderate temperatures, followed by a short sub-solvus anneal to partially recrystallize the microstructure, will eliminate microcrack initiation sites and enhance dislocation slip transfer across colony boundaries. This should simultaneously increase yield strength (via refined structural length scales) and improve room-temperature tensile ductility (by diminishing localized brittle fracture). Prior severe-deformation studies of high-entropy alloys suggest refined microstructures better resist crack propagation. An experiment to fabricate samples under these conditions and perform tensile testing at room temperature will falsify the hypothesis if no improvement in ductility or reduced microcracking is observed compared to the untreated baseline.
